III-26.explain: Most childhood upper airway infections are viral and self-limiting; the skill is spotting the few bacterial or airway-threatening ones.
III-26.hook: Upper airway = mostly viruses; hunt the bacterial and the blocked.

checks.q: What usually causes upper respiratory tract infections in children?
checks.why: Most URTIs (pharyngitis, croup, bronchitis) are viral, so antibiotics are rarely needed.

III-26.explain: Respiratory viruses dominate; group A strep is the key bacterial throat pathogen and pneumococcus leads in sinus and middle ear disease.

checks.q: Which virus is the classic cause of croup?
checks.why: Croup is laryngotracheitis caused mainly by parainfluenza; rhinovirus causes colds.

checks.q: Most frequent pathogen of bacterial sinusitis and otitis media?
checks.why: S. pneumoniae leads sinusitis and AOM; GAS is the key bacterial pharyngitis cause.

III-26.explain: Swelling blocks drainage (sinus ostia) or narrows the airway; in croup the cricoid is a rigid ring, so oedema can only shrink the lumen inward.
III-26.hook: Poiseuille: halve the radius, resistance x16.

checks.q: Why does a cold predispose to bacterial sinusitis?
checks.why: A swollen ostiomeatal complex stops drainage; stagnant secretions get colonised.

checks.q: Where is the oedema in croup that causes high airway resistance?
checks.why: The cricoid is a complete rigid ring, so subglottic oedema narrows the radius sharply.

III-26.explain: Each airway level has its own sound: subglottic croup barks and has stridor, epiglottitis drools, small airway disease wheezes.
III-26.hook: Bark = croup, drool = epiglottis, wheeze = bronchioles.

checks.q: Which feature argues against strep pharyngitis (Centor)?
checks.why: Strep: fever, exudate, tender nodes and absent cough; cough suggests a virus.

checks.q: Drooling and tripod posture in a toxic child suggest?
checks.why: Epiglottitis patients cannot swallow saliva and lean forward; croup barks instead.

checks.q: How does pertussis often present in young infants?
checks.why: Young infants often lack the whoop and present with apnoea and cyanosis.

III-26.explain: Bacterial sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis by time course; strep needs a test, and in epiglottitis examining the throat may trigger obstruction.
III-26.hook: 10 days, double dip, or severe start.

checks.q: Symptom duration suggesting bacterial sinusitis?
checks.why: Persistent symptoms beyond 10 days (or double worsening/severe onset) suggest bacterial sinusitis.

checks.q: What must you avoid in suspected epiglottitis?
checks.why: Throat examination can provoke complete obstruction; secure the airway first.

III-26.explain: Antibiotics only for the three bacterial URTIs; penicillin for strep aims at preventing rheumatic fever, and steroids shrink croup oedema.
III-26.hook: Abx trio: Strep throat, AOM, bacterial sinusitis.

checks.q: Which upper airway infection should receive antibiotics?
checks.why: University key: strep angina, AOM and acute bacterial sinusitis need antibiotics; colds do not.

checks.q: Duration of penicillin V for strep pharyngitis?
checks.why: A full 10 days eradicates GAS and prevents rheumatic fever.

checks.q: First priority in epiglottitis?
checks.why: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency; intubate in a controlled setting before anything else.

III-27.explain: AOM is acute infection behind the drum, OME is fluid without acute infection, and otitis externa is a skin infection of the canal.
III-27.hook: Media = middle ear; externa = outside canal.

checks.q: Middle ear effusion without acute infection is called?
checks.why: OME is fluid without signs of acute inflammation; AOM is acute infection.

III-27.explain: AOM bugs mirror the nasopharynx; otitis externa follows water exposure and is typically Pseudomonas.
III-27.hook: Swimmer's ear = Pseudomonas in the pool.

checks.q: Most common bacterial cause of AOM?
checks.why: Pneumococcus leads AOM, followed by non-typeable H. influenzae and Moraxella.

checks.q: Typical pathogen of otitis externa?
checks.why: Otitis externa (swimmer's ear) is classically Pseudomonas.

III-27.explain: A child's Eustachian tube is short, horizontal and floppy, so it blocks and refluxes easily; trapped fluid either infects or just dampens sound.

checks.q: Why are children prone to AOM?
checks.why: The infant tube drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal bugs reach the middle ear.

checks.q: What causes otorrhoea in AOM?
checks.why: Pus under pressure bulges the drum; perforation releases it as discharge.

checks.q: What hearing loss does OME cause?
checks.why: Fluid damps drum movement, causing conductive loss.

III-27.explain: Each condition has its sign: bulging drum in AOM, dull retracted drum with flat tympanogram in OME, tragal pain in externa.

checks.q: Typical drum appearance in AOM?
checks.why: Pus under pressure makes the drum bulge; OME drums are dull and retracted.

checks.q: Tympanogram type in OME?
checks.why: Fluid stops drum movement, giving a flat type B trace.

checks.q: Typical sign of otitis externa?
checks.why: University key: pain and/or sensitivity of the tragus; canal skin is stretched.

III-27.explain: Look at the drum; measure mobility for OME. A pushed-forward ear after AOM means spread to mastoid air cells.
III-27.hook: Ear sticks out after AOM = mastoid.

checks.q: Which test confirms OME?
checks.why: Tympanometry shows the immobile drum of an effusion.

checks.q: Protruding ear with postauricular swelling after AOM suggests?
checks.why: Spread to the mastoid pushes the pinna forward; treat with IV antibiotics and CT.

III-27.explain: Most AOM settles, so analgesia first with antibiotics for high-risk groups; OME is watched, grommets only when chronic.
III-27.hook: Grommets for glue that won't go.

checks.q: When should amoxicillin be given for AOM?
checks.why: Antibiotics for <2 y bilateral AOM or otorrhoea; otherwise analgesia and watchful waiting.

checks.q: When are grommets indicated?
checks.why: University key: chronic serous otitis media or Eustachian tube dysfunction after ~3 months.

checks.q: Treatment of otitis externa?
checks.why: Aural toilet plus topical antibiotic ± steroid drops treats a canal infection.

III-28.explain: Pneumonia fills alveoli with exudate; infection can then spread to pleura (effusion, empyema) or necrose lung (abscess).
III-28.hook: Fluid in the alveoli, pus in the pleura.

checks.q: Which is a recognised complication of pneumonia?
checks.why: Pneumonia can cause effusion, empyema and lung abscess.

III-28.explain: Pathogens follow age: birth-canal bugs in neonates, viruses in preschoolers, Mycoplasma in school-age, pneumococcus throughout.

checks.q: Commonest cause of pneumonia in preschool children overall?
checks.why: Viruses dominate under 5; GBS is a neonatal pathogen, Mycoplasma school-age.

checks.q: Most common cause of typical pneumonia?
checks.why: University key: S. pneumoniae; S. aureus suggests pneumatoceles after influenza.

III-28.explain: Filled alveoli cut compliance and create shunt, so the child breathes fast, works hard and desaturates; pleural fluid evolves from thin to fibrous.

checks.q: Why does pneumonia cause hypoxaemia?
checks.why: Perfused but unventilated alveoli create shunt.

checks.q: Final stage of a parapneumonic effusion?
checks.why: Stages: exudative, fibrinopurulent, then organising with a fibrous peel.

III-28.explain: Fast breathing is the most sensitive sign; lower-lobe pneumonia can irritate the diaphragm and mimic an abdomen; fever despite antibiotics means a collection.
III-28.hook: Fever after 48 h of antibiotics = look for pus.

checks.q: WHO tachypnoea threshold for age 1-5 years?
checks.why: ≥60 under 2 months, ≥50 at 2-12 months, ≥40 at 1-5 years.

checks.q: Why can pneumonia cause abdominal pain?
checks.why: Lower-lobe pleurisy refers pain via the diaphragm to the abdomen.

checks.q: Fever persisting after 48 h of antibiotics suggests?
checks.why: Persisting fever suggests a collection needing imaging and drainage.

III-28.explain: Pneumonia is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is for those admitted or not improving, and ultrasound shows whether pleural fluid is loculated.
III-28.hook: Treat the child, not the X-ray.

checks.q: Is a CXR routine for a child managed at home?
checks.why: Mild CAP managed at home does not need a CXR.

checks.q: SpO₂ threshold for admission?
checks.why: Admit if SpO₂ <92%, grunting, apnoea or poor feeding.

III-28.explain: Amoxicillin covers pneumococcus; severe cases go IV; thick pleural pus needs drainage and fibrinolytics to break loculations.
III-28.hook: Pus: drain it, dissolve it, then VATS.

checks.q: First-line oral antibiotic for childhood CAP?
checks.why: Amoxicillin covers pneumococcus; add a macrolide if Mycoplasma suspected.

checks.q: UK IV choice for severe childhood pneumonia?
checks.why: Severe CAP: IV ampicillin/penicillin G or ceftriaxone (US), co-amoxiclav/cefuroxime (UK).

checks.q: What dissolves thick empyema pus after drainage?
checks.why: University key: fibrinolysis (urokinase/streptokinase); VATS if it fails.

III-29.explain: These are structural defects present from birth involving the diaphragm, lung tissue or chest wall.

checks.q: Congenital lung malformations involve which structures?
checks.why: They cover diaphragmatic, parenchymal and chest wall anomalies.

III-29.explain: CDH comes from failed closure of the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal, mostly left; pectus deformities are the commonest chest wall anomalies.

checks.q: Typical location of a Bochdalek CDH?
checks.why: Bochdalek hernias are posterolateral, usually left; Morgagni are anterior.

checks.q: Two most frequent chest wall deformities?
checks.why: Pectus excavatum (sunken) and carinatum (pigeon) are the commonest.

III-29.explain: In CDH, gut in the chest stops lung growth, so hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension kill; in lobar emphysema weak cartilage lets air in but not out.
III-29.hook: Ball-valve: air in, can't get out.

checks.q: What drives mortality in CDH?
checks.why: Hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension determine survival.

checks.q: Lobe most often affected in congenital lobar emphysema?
checks.why: Deficient cartilage causes ball-valve trapping, most often left upper lobe.

III-29.explain: Abdominal contents in the chest leave a flat belly and push the heart right; a malformed lobe keeps getting infected.
III-29.hook: CDH: scaphoid belly, heart pushed right.

checks.q: Abdominal shape in CDH?
checks.why: Gut has moved into the chest, so the abdomen looks sunken.

checks.q: Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe suggests?
checks.why: A fixed malformation keeps getting infected in one place.

III-29.explain: Many are seen antenatally; CPAM connects to airways, sequestration has its own systemic artery, and pectus severity is graded by Haller index.
III-29.hook: Sequestration = separate from bronchi, fed by aorta.

checks.q: Which lesion has cysts communicating with the airway?
checks.why: CPAM cysts connect to the bronchial tree; sequestration does not.

checks.q: Usual blood supply of pulmonary sequestration?
checks.why: Sequestration has systemic arterial supply, usually from the aorta.

checks.q: Index used to grade pectus severity?
checks.why: The Haller index on CT/MRI quantifies pectus depth.

III-29.explain: In CDH bagging inflates the gut in the chest, so intubate and decompress; symptomatic lesions are resected; pectus excavatum is corrected by a bar.
III-29.hook: CDH: no bag, tube in, NG out.

checks.q: What should you avoid in suspected CDH?
checks.why: Bagging inflates the intrathoracic bowel and further compresses the lung.

checks.q: Treatment of symptomatic CPAM or sequestration?
checks.why: Symptomatic lesions are resected.

checks.q: Surgical correction of pectus excavatum?
checks.why: Nuss bar for excavatum; carinatum is treated with a compressive brace.

III-30.explain: CF is autosomal recessive; F508del misfolds CFTR so it never reaches the cell surface.
III-30.hook: F508del: Folded wrong, Fails to arrive.

checks.q: Commonest CF mutation?
checks.why: F508del (class II) causes misfolding and degradation of CFTR.

III-30.explain: About 1 in 25 Europeans carries a mutation; classes describe how CFTR fails: misfolding (II) or failed gating (III).

checks.q: Approximate CF carrier frequency in Europeans?
checks.why: Carriers ~1/25; affected births ~1/2500.

III-30.explain: Without CFTR, chloride stays in and ENaC pulls sodium and water out, drying mucus; in the sweat duct chloride cannot be reabsorbed, so sweat is salty.
III-30.hook: Lungs dry, sweat salty: same channel, opposite jobs.

checks.q: Why is airway mucus dehydrated in CF?
options: No Cl⁻ secretion and unopposed ENaC
checks.why: Absent chloride secretion plus Na⁺ absorption dries the airway surface.

checks.q: Why is CF sweat salty?
checks.why: CFTR normally reabsorbs Cl⁻ in the duct; without it salt stays in sweat.

III-30.explain: Thick secretions block gut, pancreas and airways; chronic airway infection shifts from S. aureus to Pseudomonas; salt loss causes hyponatraemia.

checks.q: Contrast enema finding in meconium ileus?
checks.why: An unused colon is tiny; plain film shows soap-bubble appearance.

checks.q: Main chronic lung pathogen in CF?
checks.why: S. aureus early, Pseudomonas becomes the main chronic pathogen.

checks.q: Which vitamins are deficient in CF?
checks.why: Fat malabsorption causes fat-soluble (ADEK) deficiency.

III-30.explain: Pancreatic damage raises IRT on newborn screen; diagnosis is confirmed by high sweat chloride.

checks.q: What does CF newborn screening measure first?
checks.why: IRT is raised on the heel-prick card, followed by a CFTR panel.

checks.q: Diagnostic sweat chloride level?
checks.why: ≥60 diagnostic; 30-59 intermediate.

III-30.explain: Clear mucus, kill bugs, replace enzymes and calories, and now correct CFTR with modulators; transplant both lungs so the native lung can't reseed infection.
III-30.hook: Dornase cuts DNA strands in pus.

checks.q: How does dornase alfa work?
checks.why: Dornase breaks down viscous extracellular DNA.

checks.q: Which drug class corrects the CFTR defect?
checks.why: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor improve CFTR function.

checks.q: Why is CF lung transplant bilateral?
options: Avoids seeding from the native lung
checks.why: A remaining infected native lung would reseed the graft.

III-31.explain: Asthma combines inflammation, twitchy airways and obstruction that reverses, which separates it from fixed airway disease.

checks.q: Which feature defines asthma obstruction?
checks.why: Asthma = chronic inflammation + hyperresponsiveness + reversible obstruction.

III-31.explain: Risk comes from atopy and environment; attacks are set off by viruses, exercise, allergens and smoke.

checks.q: Which is a risk factor for asthma?
checks.why: Atopy (eczema, rhinitis), family history, smoke, prematurity and obesity raise risk.

checks.q: Commonest trigger of acute asthma in children?
checks.why: Viral URTIs trigger most exacerbations.

III-31.explain: Th2 inflammation releases histamine and leukotrienes; bronchospasm responds to β2-agonists and oedema to steroids, while chronic inflammation remodels the airway.

checks.q: Which leukotrienes mediate asthma bronchoconstriction?
checks.why: Cysteinyl leukotrienes C4/D4/E4 constrict airways; montelukast blocks them.

checks.q: What does a β2-agonist mainly reverse?
checks.why: β2-agonists relax smooth muscle; steroids treat oedema/inflammation.

III-31.explain: Variable wheeze and night cough are typical; a silent chest means no airflow, and a normal CO2 in a tachypnoeic child means tiring.
III-31.hook: Silent chest and normal CO2 = danger.

checks.q: Typical asthma symptom timing?
checks.why: Recurrent wheeze, nocturnal cough and exercise symptoms are typical.

checks.q: What does a normal or rising PaCO2 mean in acute asthma?
checks.why: A tachypnoeic child should have low CO2; normal/rising signals tiring.

III-31.explain: Young children can't do spirometry, so diagnose clinically; from 5 years objective tests show inflammation (FeNO) and reversibility.

checks.q: How is asthma diagnosed under 5 years?
checks.why: Under-5s cannot reliably perform tests; diagnosis is clinical.

checks.q: FEV1 rise that shows reversibility?
checks.why: A ≥12% FEV1 increase after bronchodilator indicates reversibility.

III-31.explain: Inhaled steroids control inflammation and are the base of every step; acute attacks get bronchodilators plus systemic steroid, then magnesium if refractory.
III-31.hook: ICS is the foundation; magnesium is the rescue.

checks.q: Cornerstone controller in childhood asthma?
checks.why: Low-dose ICS is the base; LABA is never used alone.

checks.q: Oral steroid used in acute asthma in the UK?
checks.why: Acute: O₂, salbutamol, ipratropium, prednisolone (or dexamethasone in US).

checks.q: Add-on for severe asthma unresponsive to nebulisers?
checks.why: IV magnesium relaxes smooth muscle; then PICU.

III-32.explain: Atopy is an inherited tendency to make IgE to harmless antigens via Th2 responses.

checks.q: Atopy is a genetic tendency to produce which antibody?
checks.why: Atopy is a Th2-driven tendency to make IgE.

III-32.explain: Atopic diseases appear in sequence; barrier defects such as filaggrin loss let allergens sensitise through skin.

checks.q: Order of the atopic march (university key)?
checks.why: Exam key: food allergy - atopic dermatitis - asthma - allergic rhinitis (literature often puts eczema first).

checks.q: Which gene mutation breaks the skin barrier in atopy?
checks.why: Filaggrin loss-of-function allows epicutaneous sensitisation.

III-32.explain: IgE arms mast cells; allergen cross-links IgE causing instant mediator release, while IL-5-driven eosinophils cause late chronic inflammation.

checks.q: What triggers mast cell degranulation in allergy?
checks.why: Allergen bridges two IgE molecules, releasing histamine and leukotrienes.

checks.q: Which cytokine recruits eosinophils?
checks.why: IL-5 drives eosinophils and the late-phase reaction.

III-32.explain: IgE reactions are fast (minutes to 2 h) and systemic; non-IgE reactions are slow and mostly gut or skin.

checks.q: Time to onset of IgE-mediated food reactions?
checks.why: IgE reactions are immediate: urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, anaphylaxis.

checks.q: Which is a non-IgE food reaction?
checks.why: FPIES, proctocolitis and eczema flares are delayed non-IgE reactions.

III-32.explain: Parents over-report food allergy; specific IgE shows sensitisation not allergy, so elimination then re-challenge is the test.

checks.q: True frequency of childhood food allergy (after re-challenge)?
checks.why: University key: parents report ~7-10%, reality ~1-2%.

checks.q: Recommended method to diagnose food allergy?
checks.why: Specific IgE is not totally reliable; elimination and re-challenge confirm.

III-32.explain: Avoid the allergen with dietary support; anaphylaxis needs IM adrenaline in the thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed.

checks.q: Formula for a cow's milk-allergic infant?
checks.why: Goat's milk cross-reacts; use extensively hydrolysed formula.

checks.q: IM adrenaline dose in anaphylaxis?
checks.why: 10 µg/kg (0.01 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL) IM in anterolateral thigh, repeat at 5 min.

III-33.explain: Heart failure means output cannot meet demand, causing congestion; decompensation means shock and collapse.

checks.q: What defines decompensated heart failure?
checks.why: Decompensated HF progresses to low output, shock and collapse.

III-33.explain: Timing points to cause: duct-dependent left lesions in week 1, shunts at 4-8 weeks as PVR falls, myocardial disease later.

checks.q: Cause of heart failure in the first week of life?
checks.why: HLHS and coarctation decompensate as the duct closes.

checks.q: When does a large VSD cause heart failure?
checks.why: Falling pulmonary vascular resistance increases the left-to-right shunt.

checks.q: Which is a later-onset cause of heart failure?
checks.why: Myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, Kawasaki and anaemia cause later HF.

III-33.explain: Low output triggers sympathetic and RAAS compensation (sweat, tachycardia, fluid retention); back-pressure congests lungs and liver.
III-33.hook: Back-up behind the left = lungs; right = liver.

checks.q: Why do infants with heart failure sweat?
checks.why: Low output drives sympathetic drive: tachycardia and sweating.

checks.q: Raised systemic venous pressure causes?
checks.why: Systemic venous congestion enlarges the liver; pulmonary congestion causes tachypnoea.

III-33.explain: Infants show HF as feeding difficulty with sweating and poor growth; the liver edge is the most reliable congestion sign.
III-33.hook: Infant HF: feeds, sweats, fails to grow.

checks.q: Typical feeding sign of infant heart failure?
checks.why: Feeding is exercise for infants; they tire, sweat and fail to thrive.

checks.q: Most reliable sign of heart failure in an infant?
checks.why: Infant oedema and JVP are hard to see; the liver is reliable.

III-33.explain: Echo identifies the lesion; bloods and gas assess severity and organ perfusion.
III-33.hook: Echo for cause; lactate for severity.

checks.q: Which test defines the cause of heart failure?
checks.why: Echo shows structure and function; CXR shows only cardiomegaly.

checks.q: Which blood marker rises with ventricular stretch?
checks.why: BNP/NT-proBNP is released from stretched myocardium.

III-33.explain: Reduce workload and fluid, feed calories, block neurohormones; reopen the duct with PGE1 in neonatal duct-dependent lesions.
III-33.hook: Week-1 failure: open the duct with PGE1.

checks.q: Calorie target for infant heart failure feeds?
checks.why: High-calorie NG feeds up to 150 kcal/kg/day support growth.

checks.q: Which diuretic spares potassium?
checks.why: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and conserves K⁺.

checks.q: Drug for a first-week duct-dependent lesion?
checks.why: PGE1 keeps the duct open; NSAIDs would close it.

III-34.explain: Cyanotic CHD causes central cyanosis by right-to-left mixing; remember the 5 Ts.
III-34.hook: 5 Ts: Tetralogy, TGA, Truncus, Tricuspid, TAPVR.

checks.q: Mnemonic for cyanotic congenital heart disease?
checks.why: Tetralogy, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR.

III-34.explain: Cyanosis arises either from reduced pulmonary flow with R→L shunt, or from parallel circulations as in TGA.
III-34.hook: TGA = day 1 blue; Fallot = later blue.

checks.q: Which lesion has reduced pulmonary blood flow?
checks.why: Fallot's RVOT obstruction reduces pulmonary flow with R→L shunt.

checks.q: Commonest cyanotic lesion in the first days?
checks.why: TGA presents with profound early cyanosis.

III-34.explain: Cyanosis needs enough deoxygenated haemoglobin; Fallot spells increase R→L shunting; chronic hypoxia drives polycythaemia and clubbing.
III-34.hook: Spell = more blood bypasses the lungs.

checks.q: Deoxygenated haemoglobin needed for visible cyanosis?
checks.why: Central cyanosis appears at about 3-5 g/dL deoxyhaemoglobin.

checks.q: Which is part of tetralogy of Fallot?
checks.why: RVOT obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta and RV hypertrophy.

checks.q: Chronic hypoxia leads to?
checks.why: Hypoxia raises EPO, causing polycythaemia and clubbing.

III-34.explain: In a tet spell less blood crosses the RVOT so the murmur fades; TGA babies are very blue, often with no murmur.

checks.q: What happens to the Fallot murmur during a spell?
checks.why: Less flow through the obstructed RVOT means a quieter murmur.

checks.q: Classic CXR appearance in TGA?
checks.why: TGA: egg on a string; Fallot: boot-shaped; supracardiac TAPVR: snowman.

III-34.explain: Oxygen does not raise PaO2 when blood bypasses the lungs; pulse oximetry screening catches critical CHD.

checks.q: Result of hyperoxia test in cardiac cyanosis?
checks.why: Shunted blood bypasses the lungs, so 100% O₂ barely raises PaO2.

checks.q: Sites for pulse-oximetry CHD screening?
checks.why: Pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (foot) saturations are compared.

III-34.explain: A blue newborn not improving on oxygen gets PGE1 to keep pulmonary or mixing flow; tet spells are treated by raising SVR; TGA needs early arterial switch.
III-34.hook: Knee-chest squeezes arteries, pushes blood to lungs.

checks.q: Blue newborn not improving on oxygen: give?
checks.why: PGE1 maintains ductal flow; watch for apnoea.

checks.q: Why does knee-chest position help a tet spell?
checks.why: Higher SVR reduces R→L shunting across the VSD.

checks.q: Definitive surgery for TGA?
checks.why: Arterial switch in the first 2-3 weeks after septostomy if needed.

III-35.explain: Acyanotic CHD is either a left-to-right shunt or an obstruction to outflow.

checks.q: Two groups of non-cyanotic CHD?
checks.why: Acyanotic CHD comprises left-to-right shunts and obstructive lesions.

III-35.explain: VSD is commonest; syndromes link to specific lesions (Down-AVSD, Turner-coarctation, Noonan-pulmonary stenosis).

checks.q: Commonest congenital heart defect?
checks.why: VSD is the commonest CHD.

checks.q: Coarctation is associated with which syndrome?
checks.why: Turner: coarctation; Noonan: pulmonary stenosis; Down: AVSD.

III-35.explain: Chronic pulmonary overflow remodels pulmonary vessels until the shunt reverses; a small VSD has a big pressure gradient, so it is loud.

checks.q: Reversal of a long-standing L→R shunt is called?
checks.why: Pulmonary vascular disease reverses flow, causing cyanosis.

checks.q: Why is a small VSD often louder?
checks.why: Fast, turbulent flow through a small hole makes a loud murmur.

III-35.explain: Four key CHD signs; specific clues pin the lesion: fixed split S2 (ASD), machinery murmur (PDA), weak femorals (coarctation).

checks.q: Which is one of the 4 key signs of CHD?
checks.why: University key: murmur, heart failure, cyanosis, peripheral pulse abnormalities.

checks.q: Fixed wide splitting of S2 suggests?
checks.why: ASD gives a fixed widely split S2; PDA a continuous machinery murmur.

checks.q: Femoral pulses in coarctation?
checks.why: Obstruction distal to the arm vessels weakens and delays femorals.

III-35.explain: Echo diagnoses structure; murmur site and character suggest the lesion; innocent murmurs are soft, systolic and change with posture.
III-35.hook: Innocent: soft, systolic, shifts with posture.

checks.q: Investigation to diagnose congenital heart defects?
checks.why: Echocardiography defines congenital anatomy.

checks.q: Holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border?
checks.why: LLSB holosystolic murmur = VSD.

checks.q: Which feature suggests an innocent murmur?
checks.why: Innocent murmurs are soft, systolic, postural with no other signs.

III-35.explain: Large VSDs are closed early before pulmonary vascular disease; ASDs by catheter device at preschool age; prostaglandin keeps the duct open in critical coarctation, NSAIDs close a preterm PDA.
III-35.hook: Open the duct: PGE1; close it: NSAID.

checks.q: Typical age for ASD catheter closure?
checks.why: ASD device closure at 3-5 years; large VSD surgery in first months.

checks.q: Drug to close a preterm PDA?
checks.why: Ibuprofen, indomethacin or paracetamol close the duct; PGE1 keeps it open.

III-36.explain: Cardiomyopathy is primary heart muscle disease; dilated is the commonest type in children.

checks.q: Commonest type of childhood cardiomyopathy?
checks.why: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most common.

III-36.explain: DCM follows myocyte injury (virus, anthracycline, dystrophy); HCM is a dominant sarcomere disorder or transient in infants of diabetic mothers.

checks.q: Chemotherapy drug linked to DCM?
checks.why: Anthracyclines (doxorubicin) cause dose-related cardiotoxicity.

checks.q: Inheritance of HCM?
checks.why: HCM is usually AD sarcomere gene mutation.

III-36.explain: Three failures: DCM can't empty, HCM can't fill and obstructs outflow, RCM can't stretch so atria balloon.

checks.q: Main haemodynamic problem in DCM?
checks.why: Dilated ventricle can't empty: low EF.

checks.q: Feared complication of HCM?
checks.why: Dynamic LVOT obstruction and arrhythmia cause sudden death.

checks.q: Characteristic finding in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
checks.why: Stiff ventricles back pressure into very large atria.

III-36.explain: DCM looks like infant heart failure; HCM murmur gets louder when preload falls (Valsalva, standing) because the outflow narrows.

checks.q: Which is a sign of DCM in an infant?
checks.why: DCM: tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating, hepatomegaly, gallop.

checks.q: HCM murmur with Valsalva?
checks.why: Lower preload shrinks the LV cavity and worsens obstruction.

III-36.explain: Echo shows dilation or hypertrophy; because HCM is inherited, relatives must be screened.

checks.q: Key imaging for cardiomyopathy?
checks.why: Echo shows low-EF dilated LV or hypertrophy.

checks.q: Who should be screened after a cardiomyopathy diagnosis?
checks.why: Genetic cardiomyopathies need first-degree relative screening.

III-36.explain: DCM uses heart-failure drugs that prolong survival; HCM avoids anything reducing preload or increasing contractility; RCM goes early to transplant.
III-36.hook: HCM: slow and full; avoid inotropes.

checks.q: Which beta-blocker is used in paediatric DCM?
checks.why: Carvedilol plus ACE-i/ARB and spironolactone improve survival.

checks.q: What should be avoided in HCM?
checks.why: Inotropes, vasodilators and excess diuretics worsen LVOT obstruction.

checks.q: Treatment of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
checks.why: RCM has poor prognosis and early pulmonary hypertension, so early transplant.

III-37.explain: Myocarditis inflames heart muscle; pericarditis inflames the sac, sometimes with effusion.

checks.q: Pericarditis is inflammation of?
checks.why: Pericarditis affects the pericardium ± effusion.

III-37.explain: Viruses dominate both; purulent pericarditis is usually Staph aureus.

checks.q: Commonest cause of myocarditis in children?
checks.why: Enteroviruses, adenovirus and parvovirus B19 are typical.

checks.q: Usual cause of purulent pericarditis?
checks.why: Purulent pericarditis is classically S. aureus.

III-37.explain: Losing myocytes lowers stroke volume, so heart rate rises; in tamponade fluid pressure stops ventricular filling.

checks.q: Compensation for reduced stroke volume in myocarditis?
checks.why: Output = SV × HR, so HR rises.

checks.q: Why does stroke volume fall in tamponade?
checks.why: Pericardial fluid pressure prevents diastolic filling.

III-37.explain: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever flags myocarditis; pericardial pain eases leaning forward; tamponade shows Beck triad and pulsus paradoxus.
III-37.hook: Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mmHg fall on inspiration.

checks.q: Clue to myocarditis in a febrile child?
options: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
checks.why: Disproportionate tachycardia suggests myocardial involvement.

checks.q: Posture relieving pericarditis pain?
checks.why: Leaning forward reduces pericardial stretch.

checks.q: Systolic fall defining pulsus paradoxus?
checks.why: Inspiratory fall >10 mmHg in systolic pressure.

III-37.explain: Myocarditis shows low voltages and raised troponin; pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression.
III-37.hook: Pericarditis ECG: smiley ST, sad PR.

checks.q: ECG finding in myocarditis?
checks.why: Sinus tachycardia and low-voltage QRS are typical.

checks.q: ECG hallmark of pericarditis?
checks.why: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression.

III-37.explain: Myocarditis is supportive with cautious fluids and rest from sport; pericarditis gets NSAID and colchicine; tamponade and pus need drainage.

checks.q: How long to avoid competitive sport after myocarditis?
checks.why: Exercise can trigger arrhythmia; no competitive sport for 3-6 months.

checks.q: Treatment of viral pericarditis?
checks.why: NSAID + colchicine; tamponade needs pericardiocentesis.

checks.q: Management of purulent pericarditis?
options: Surgical drainage plus IV antistaphylococcal antibiotics
checks.why: Pus must be drained with IV anti-staphylococcal cover.

III-38.explain: IE is infection of the endocardium, typically on valves or defects where flow is turbulent.

checks.q: Usual site of infective endocarditis?
checks.why: IE infects the endocardium, usually on valves or defects.

III-38.explain: Highest risk is prosthetic material, prosthetic valves and previous IE; lines seed normal neonatal hearts; viridans strep is subacute, S. aureus acute.
III-38.hook: Viridans = slow, from teeth; aureus = aggressive.

checks.q: Which patient has the highest IE risk?
checks.why: Prosthetic material/valves and previous IE carry the highest risk.

checks.q: IE risk factor in neonates with normal hearts?
checks.why: Central lines seed bacteraemia onto normal endocardium.

checks.q: Organism of subacute IE after dental bacteraemia?
checks.why: Viridans streptococci cause subacute IE; S. aureus causes acute IE.

III-38.explain: Turbulent jets damage endothelium, platelet-fibrin clumps form and bacteria seed them; fragments embolise and immune complexes cause nephritis and Osler/Roth lesions.

checks.q: What forms on damaged endothelium before infection?
checks.why: A sterile platelet-fibrin vegetation is then seeded by bacteraemia.

checks.q: Immune complexes in IE cause?
checks.why: Immune complex lesions: GN, Osler nodes, Roth spots.

III-38.explain: Suspect IE with prolonged fever and a new murmur; Osler nodes hurt (immune), Janeway lesions don't (embolic).

checks.q: Classic IE presentation?
checks.why: FROM JANE: fever, Roth, Osler, murmur, Janeway, anaemia, nail, emboli.

checks.q: Painful finger-pulp nodules in IE are?
checks.why: Osler nodes are painful; Janeway lesions are painless palmar macules.

III-38.explain: Diagnosis rests on organisms in blood and a vegetation on echo; take several cultures before antibiotics.

checks.q: Basis of IE diagnosis?
checks.why: University key: haemoculture and echocardiography.

checks.q: Blood cultures before antibiotics in suspected IE?
checks.why: At least three sets from separate venepunctures.

III-38.explain: Long IV bactericidal therapy is needed to sterilise avascular vegetations; prophylaxis is a single amoxicillin dose before dental work in high-risk children.
III-38.hook: Prophylaxis: one dose, an hour before the dentist.

checks.q: Duration of IV antibiotics for IE?
checks.why: Vegetations are poorly penetrated, so 4-6 weeks IV bactericidal therapy.

checks.q: Regimen for IE with prosthetic material?
checks.why: Prosthetic material: vancomycin + gentamicin; surgery for HF or emboli.

checks.q: IE prophylaxis before dental work in high-risk children?
checks.why: A single oral dose 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

III-39.explain: Malabsorption splits into maldigestion (no enzymes) and mucosal disease; coeliac is a permanent gluten-triggered immune enteropathy.

checks.q: Pancreatic insufficiency causes which type of malabsorption?
checks.why: Lack of enzymes is maldigestion; mucosal disease is malabsorption.

checks.q: What triggers coeliac disease?
checks.why: Coeliac is a permanent immune enteropathy triggered by gluten.

III-39.explain: CF is the main pancreatic cause; mucosal causes include coeliac, CMPA, Giardia, Crohn; coeliac requires HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and clusters with autoimmune and chromosomal conditions.

checks.q: Commonest cause of pancreatic insufficiency in children?
checks.why: CF is the commonest paediatric cause.

checks.q: Which parasite causes mucosal malabsorption?
checks.why: Giardia damages the small bowel mucosa.

checks.q: HLA types required for coeliac disease?
checks.why: Coeliac essentially requires HLA-DQ2 or DQ8.

III-39.explain: Gliadin triggers T-cell damage flattening villi with deep crypts and lymphocytes; lost surface area means fat malabsorption carries ADEK out.
III-39.hook: Flat villi, deep crypts, many lymphocytes.

checks.q: Classic coeliac histology?
checks.why: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis.

III-39.explain: Classic infants have diarrhoea, distension and wasting after gluten is introduced; older children often show extraintestinal clues.

checks.q: Typical age of classical coeliac presentation?
checks.why: Classical coeliac follows gluten introduction at 6 m-2 y.

checks.q: Skin manifestation of coeliac disease?
checks.why: University key includes dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring disease).

III-39.explain: Test anti-tTG IgA with total IgA while eating gluten; IgA must be at least 0.2 g/l; biopsy can be skipped if the university's three criteria are met.

checks.q: First-line coeliac test?
checks.why: Serology on a gluten-containing diet with total IgA.

checks.q: Minimum IgA to read tTG/EMA reliably?
checks.why: University key: 0.2 g/l; below this use IgG-based tests.

checks.q: Which is required to avoid biopsy (university criteria)?
checks.why: Symptoms + tTG AND EMA + HLA-DQ2/DQ8 (ESPGHAN 2012, as the university uses).

III-39.explain: Coeliac needs lifelong strict gluten avoidance, with antibodies falling to confirm adherence; CMPA uses hydrolysed protein formulas.
III-39.hook: Antibodies tell you if they cheat.

checks.q: How is coeliac adherence monitored?
checks.why: Falling tTG antibodies reflect gluten-free adherence.

checks.q: Formula for severe CMPA?
checks.why: Extensively hydrolysed formula first; amino-acid formula if severe.

III-40.explain: The mouth's problems are mostly infections; oesophageal disease includes reflux, EoE, achalasia, TEF and foreign bodies.

checks.q: Most mouth diseases in children are?
checks.why: Oral cavity disease in children is mostly infectious.

III-40.explain: Each oral infection has its bug: HSV-1, coxsackie A, Candida; TEF is part of VACTERL, usually atresia with distal fistula.

checks.q: Cause of herpangina?
checks.why: Herpangina is coxsackie A; gingivostomatitis is HSV-1.

checks.q: Commonest TEF type?
checks.why: Oesophageal atresia with distal TEF accounts for ~85%.

III-40.explain: Allergic eosinophilic inflammation scars the oesophagus causing food impaction; button batteries generate current and burn through tissue fast.

checks.q: Typical EoE complication?
checks.why: Rings and strictures cause food impaction.

checks.q: How fast can a button battery burn the oesophagus?
checks.why: Battery current causes tissue necrosis within about 2 hours.

III-40.explain: Gingivostomatitis involves front gums and mouth; herpangina only the soft palate; reflux usually resolves by toddlerhood; TEF chokes with feeds.

checks.q: Where are lesions in herpangina?
checks.why: Herpangina is posterior; HSV gingivostomatitis is anterior with swollen gums.

checks.q: Age by which physiological reflux resolves?
checks.why: Physiological infant reflux resolves by 12-18 months.

checks.q: Typical symptom of achalasia?
checks.why: Achalasia causes dysphagia and regurgitation; TEF chokes newborns.

III-40.explain: EoE is defined histologically; achalasia by barium and manometry; TEF by an NG tube that coils in the pouch.

checks.q: EoE biopsy threshold?
checks.why: At least 15 eosinophils per high-power field.

checks.q: Barium appearance of achalasia?
checks.why: Bird's beak taper with absent peristalsis on manometry.

checks.q: Finding suggesting pure oesophageal atresia?
checks.why: No fistula means no air reaches the gut.

III-40.explain: Antivirals work early in HSV; surgery treats severe reflux and achalasia; TEF needs repair and screening for VACTERL; swallowed objects lodged in the oesophagus need urgent endoscopy.
III-40.hook: Myotomy for achalasia; wrap for reflux.

checks.q: Time window for aciclovir in gingivostomatitis?
checks.why: Aciclovir helps if started within 72 hours.

checks.q: Surgery for achalasia?
checks.why: Heller myotomy divides the LOS; fundoplication treats reflux.

checks.q: Swallowed coin in the oesophagus: management?
checks.why: Per notes: emergency endoscopy within 2 hours (strictly urgent mainly for batteries).
